key_clinical_evidence: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Recent major surgery is a contraindication to IV tPA but not necessarily to mechanical thrombectomy
Iatrogenic carotid dissection can present weeks after cardiac surgery; recurrent TIAs in a postoperative patient demand vessel imaging
Both dissection and postoperative AF can co-occur — comprehensive workup is needed
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kenji Takahashi is a 70-year-old right-handed man who presents to the emergency department with persistent right-sided hemiparesis that began approximately three hours ago. He has a significant recent surgical history, having undergone total aortic arch replacement for a distal aortic arch aneurysm approximately six weeks prior to this presentation. His postoperative course was initially uncomplicated, and he was discharged from the surgical service two weeks after the operation in stable condition. Beginning approximately two weeks ago, he began experiencing recurrent episodes of transient right-sided weakness involving his arm and leg, each lasting between 30 minutes and several hours before spontaneously resolving. He reports approximately five such episodes over the past two weeks, each following a similar pattern with sudden onset weakness and mild slurring of speech that would gradually improve. He was seen by his primary care physician after the second episode, and a follow-up was scheduled with his vascular surgeon, but no urgent workup was initiated at that time. Today at approximately 09:00, while eating breakfast, he experienced the sudden onset of right arm weakness causing him to drop his chopsticks, followed rapidly by difficulty with his right leg and mild difficulty speaking clearly. Unlike previous episodes, the symptoms have not improved over the past three hours. His wife drove him to the emergency department, arriving at 12:05. He denies any headache, visual disturbances, chest pain, or loss of consciousness. He reports no fever, recent infection, or medication changes. His postoperative imaging at the time of his surgery had noted a finding involving the left common carotid artery adjacent to the vascular graft, but he was told it was being managed conservatively.
